questions.prompt: Which sentence is the strongest results statement?
options: The planner is faster than the baseline in most of the cases that we ran.
The planner takes 12.1 s (s.d. 0.8, n=10) versus 14.6 s (s.d. 1.1, n=10) for the baseline on map A.
The planner is significantly faster than the baseline on the maps that we tested.
The planner is much faster than the baseline, as the whole evaluation clearly shows.
questions.explanation: It has a metric, a comparison, spread, n and conditions.

questions.prompt: In what order should a results paragraph usually proceed?
options: Limitations first, then the results, and the claim only at the end.
Method details, background, then the result, and finally one limitation.
The result only; every other detail belongs in the appendix.
Claim with key number, evidence and uncertainty, interpretation, limitation.
questions.explanation: Lead with the claim so the reader knows what to look for, then show the support and the boundary.

questions.prompt: Five runs give times 12, 15, 11, 14, 13 s. What is the sample sd? Give 2 decimals.
For the five times 12, 15, 11, 14, 13 s, what is the lower end of the 95% CI of the mean (t = 2.776 for 4 df)? Give 2 decimals.
A script reports spread with the population formula (divide by n). For runs 70, 74, 72, 76 what does it print, 2 decimals? (The correct sample sd is 2.58.)
Two groups succeed 37/50 and 30/50 episodes. What is the difference in success proportion (first minus second)? Give 2 decimals.
For those groups (37/50 and 30/50), what is the unpooled standard error of the difference? Give 3 decimals.
Two groups both have mean 70 and the same bar-chart error bars, but one is [50,50,50,90,90,90] and the other [60,65,70,70,75,80]. What does this show?
options: The groups are equivalent for every purpose, since mean and error bars match.
Bars and error bars show only a mean and a spread, so different distributions look identical; show the points.
The bar chart is correct as it is, and no further detail would add any value.
Error bars are always misleading, so they should never be drawn on a bar chart.
questions.explanation: Showing individual points reveals a two-cluster distribution that a bar hides.

questions.prompt: A caption reads 'Fig 3: Results.' Which improvement is most useful?
options: Move the caption into the appendix so that the main text stays short.
State what is plotted, the metric and units, n, the error bars, and the take-away.
Add the date of the experiment, which is the only missing information.
Make the caption font bigger so that the figure can be read at a glance.
questions.explanation: A caption should let the figure be understood on its own.

questions.prompt: A bar chart axis starts at 90 and the bars show 92 and 99. By what factor does the second bar appear taller than the first? Give 2 decimals.
Rewrite this sentence so it is a testable, honest claim: 'Our SLAM system is robust and accurate in all environments.' Invent plausible numbers and conditions.
rubric: Names a metric (e.g. absolute trajectory error in cm) with value and spread.
Names the tested environments and number of runs and a baseline.
Adds a specific limitation (conditions not tested).
questions.explanation: Rubric-guided: compare your answer with each rubric point; this question is not automatically graded.

questions.prompt: Give two limitations of a paper whose only evidence is 5 seeds in one simulator, one about generality and one about statistics, and for each say what additional experiment would address it.
rubric: Generality: one simulator/robot/environment family, tested by a second simulator or hardware.
Statistics: small n gives wide intervals, addressed by more seeds (n from the sample-size formula).
Both tied to what could change the conclusion.
questions.explanation: Rubric-guided: compare your answer with each rubric point; this question is not automatically graded.

questions.prompt: Write a unit test (code or description) for a function fmt_result(xs) that returns 'mean +/- sd (n=...)' and would catch the population-sd bug.
rubric: Uses a small hand-computed input such as [70, 74, 72, 76] with expected sd 2.6 (not 2.2).
Checks that n appears in the output.
Notes an edge case (n=1 has no sample sd) and what the function should do.
questions.explanation: Rubric-guided: compare your answer with each rubric point; this question is not automatically graded.
